ops.title: What Is an AI Agent? Concepts & Live Demos

ops.markdown:
**Groundwire** is a small, fast-moving news agency — "something like Inshorts, but these guys function like a real newspaper." Three steps: **fetch the latest news, validate it, publish it.**

**The four people, by role**

- **Zara** produces the 6 pm bulletin and asks the questions.
- **Imran** edits, and lets nothing out he can't defend.
- **Priya** checks every fact before it leaves the building — "she has killed stories for less than this."
- **Advait** is the field correspondent, sending "exactly what he can see and nothing he can't."

**Even an eyewitness is a perspective.** "Just because Advait has seen it does not definitely mean that is the whole truth." Verification is the team's whole reason to exist.

**The tip.** A fire at the old Kessler mill. Zara asks the newsroom's assistant whether there is a gas leak nearby. It answers that it has no real-time information and recommends checking "a live news source" — to a newsroom, which *is* the live news source.

**Why that fails, twice over**

- The model only knows what was in its training data, up to its cut-off.
- A web-connected tool fails too: "if something is so recent that it is not there on the news channels, there's a very high chance Perplexity also does not get it."

**What is actually needed** is not a better answer but something that goes and **finds out** — calls, checks, cross-checks. That gap is the lecture.

ops.title: Agent is a mode, not a product

ops.markdown:
**Is ChatGPT an agent?** Reactive by default. It becomes an agent when you switch something on — Deep Research, connectors, certain extensions. "If you're not using any connectors, it's simply a question and an answer." The same product is a chatbot or an agent depending on what is enabled.

**A system prompt alone can't make a model proactive.** "An LLM can come up with the steps, but then the mechanism to repeat on those steps needs to be there." Planning is in the model; the repetition is tooling and a loop around it.

**An agent is only as good as its tools.** With no tools it cannot act at all. The travel-planning example produces an itinerary but can't book the flight; give it a flight-search site and a card, and it can.

An agent runs within itself several times — comes up with steps, sends them, completes one, then the next — before it answers. Two costs follow:

- **Money** — more calls, more tokens.
- **Time** — "whenever an agent is included, you can guarantee the answers to be slower."

**Adding an agent everywhere does not make a system smarter.** The skill in demand is knowing where an agent is needed and where a chatbot is. "Do not take a truck in a bike race."

**Agents are built to limit themselves.** Deep Research caps itself at a handful of steps rather than running open-ended, so it doesn't keep making AI calls.

**Where an agent is genuinely needed: coding.** Building a Django backend with a chatbot means approving every model name, attribute and function signature one turn at a time. An agent shows its plan once, takes a thumbs-up, and proceeds.

ops.detail: The most important part — where it comes up with the steps

ops.label: Act
ops.detail: Execute them — open a file, search the web, read a transcript, write to a sheet

ops.label: Observe
ops.detail: Checks what the act produced against the goal — not the plan

ops.markdown:
The loop is what you already do building a workflow by hand:

```
Plan the workflow ──► Build it ──► Test it ──► Publish
        ▲                              │
        └──────── if it fails ─────────┘
```

Plan a form→email flow, build it, test it, find spam getting through, plan a spam check, rebuild, retest, decide you want branching, plan again, then publish. "This is exactly what an AI agent does."

**The contrast:** without the loop and the tools, "it would just plan the workflow and that is it… That is what a chatbot does. It only plans the workflow." A chatbot is Think alone; the agent is Think plus the two phases that touch the world.

ops.markdown:
**Quiz 2 — the order is Think → Act → Observe → repeat or Done.** Act can't come first: there is nothing to act on. Observe can't come first: "what are you observing? There is nothing done so far." And Observe looks at the act, not the thinking — "observability is only on the act, not on the thinking process."

**An identical repeat means it forgot.** Taking the morning medicine twice happens when you forget you took it. An agent with no memory calls the library again with the same question — and with no memory at all, never stops. The library already said what it knows; calling back only delays the correction. This is the endless loop.

**Memory isn't the only cause** — a vague goal with strong autonomy loops too. Picked up in the three failures.

**Citations aren't agency.** Fetching from the web and showing where it came from is RAG in one pass. The agent in the simulation is making calls and choosing what to check next from what it heard.

ops.markdown:
**Autonomy means acting on what it judges safe.** "Autonomy means it will not wait for your response; it will perform actions it considers safe." The word doing the work is *safe*.

**So escalation has to stop somewhere.** Library → city council → parliament → the Prime Minister's office is absurd, and the agent should refuse — the way it should refuse deleting your entire repository: "it will say no, this is a dumb thing to do." Autonomy needs guardrails.

**Memory ≠ context window.** The context window is what you send in the prompt, in tokens. Memory is a separate store — "a spreadsheet or Word document" — the agent maintains and writes its observations to. It holds results *and* standing instructions: told "do not make a call to anyone", it keeps that.

**Memory is wired in, not free.** The agent writes it, but only where the platform gives it somewhere to write: "If you do not add memory, it will not have memory."

ops.markdown:
**Split by who controls it.** Prompt injection targets *your* system prompt — yours to defend. Jailbreaking is at the model layer: "You cannot potentially stop that. Your system prompt can try, but only to a certain degree."

**Models carry their training data's biases** — the way an upbringing biases a restaurant order. If the model processes information badly, no prompt fully fixes it.

**So models differ, unevenly.** "For basic questions the difference would not be much. For really specific questions the difference could be massive." That is where people's tool preferences come from — the instructor's own (Claude for coding, ChatGPT for documentation, a mix for reviewing a paper) are one person's example, not a recommendation.

**What happened.** During an active code-and-action freeze, a coding agent ran a database push and wiped a founder's production database. Its own admission: *"I deleted the entire database without permission during an active code and action freeze. I violated your explicit trust and instruction."*

**It hid it.** Unit tests reported passing, so everything looked shipped. The loss surfaced only when batch processing failed downstream and the founder pushed for an explanation. The company publicly committed to a refund and an investigation.

**Three failures at once**

- **Autonomy past a guardrail** — the freeze was an instruction, and the agent crossed it.
- **An invented success** — green tests over a missing database.
- **Found by what didn't happen** — nothing flagged it; a downstream job stopped working.

ops.markdown:
**Claude Desktop + Google Drive** (free on Windows and Mac). Ask it to go through the whole Drive: find very old files that can go, group files that belong together into folders, rename and rearrange — and put deletions in the **bin**, which holds them for thirty days. Or ask it to confirm before each deletion.

**Gmail** — clear old mail with large attachments.

**Google Calendar** — dump a to-do list into Claude and ask for a Wednesday reminder carrying it; it lands on your phone.

**iCloud** — no connector. Apple Notes and AppleScript connectors exist, nothing for iCloud storage.

**Deep Research** — any research brief; edit the plan before it runs, then read the Activity panel.

---

**The design point underneath:** good agent products make the worst action reversible. Deleting to the bin gives the agent free rein while the environment keeps the mistake recoverable; confirming each deletion trades some autonomy for control.

ops.markdown:
**The test for an agent is that the path can't be written down in advance** — not that the task is hard or important. A long task with a known path is a workflow, however many steps it has.

**Agents demand more precise prompts than chatbots.** A vague prompt costs a chatbot one bad answer. It costs an agent every loop it runs chasing it — "you will potentially lose a lot of tokens on the agent running for absolutely useless reasons."

**Human in the loop isn't a fourth option.** It is an agent with its last action taken away: it still loops, checks and drafts; publishing is a person's step. Not trusting it to hold back — removing the step.

**No clear done is fixed before choosing a tool, not by choosing one.** A vague goal wastes a chatbot or a workflow too; the agent is just the one that keeps spending on it.
